compare_package_downloads.description: Put several packages' downloads side by side over the same period, ranked, each with its share of the group's total. Use it to settle 'which of these is actually used?' in one step. A name npm has never seen is reported separately rather than failing the comparison, so one typo does not lose the answer.
compare_package_downloads.name: compare_package_downloads

parameters.description: The packages to compare, up to 256. Scoped names include the scope.
parameters.name: packages

parameters.description: How far back to count. Ignored when a start and end date are set. Defaults to the last 7 days.
parameters.name: period

parameters.description: The first day to count, for a period the list above does not cover. Set both dates or neither. npm's counts begin on 2015-01-10 and one query may span at most 18 months.
parameters.name: start_date

parameters.description: The last day to count. Set both dates or neither.
parameters.name: end_date

parameters.description: How to order the packages in the answer.
parameters.name: sort

options.label: The order the packages were listed in

get_dist_tags.description: See which version each of a package's release channels points at right now. A channel, which npm calls a dist-tag, is what 'npm install package@next' resolves through, so this is the one-request way to answer 'has the beta moved?' or 'what does latest point at today?'.

get_dist_tags.name: get_dist_tags

parameters.description: The npm package to look up, exactly as it is installed. Scoped names include the scope.
parameters.name: package

get_download_trend.description: Get a package's downloads day by day over a period, together with what the series says: the busiest and quietest days, the daily average, and whether the second half of the window ran ahead of the first. That last comparison is what turns a download count into 'rising', 'steady' or 'falling', which is the thing worth alerting on.
get_download_trend.display_str_template: Get the download trend for the npm package {0}.
get_download_trend.name: get_download_trend

parameters.description: The npm package to look up, exactly as it is installed. Scoped names include the scope.

parameters.description: How far back to count. Ignored when a start and end date are set. Defaults to the last 7 days.

parameters.description: The first day to count, for a period the list above does not cover. Set both dates or neither. npm's counts begin on 2015-01-10 and one query may span at most 18 months.
parameters.name: start_date

parameters.description: The last day to count. Set both dates or neither.
parameters.name: end_date

get_package.description: Look up an npm package: what it does, who maintains it, what licence it carries, where its source and issue tracker live, which release channels it publishes to, how many versions it has, and when it was first and last published. This is the overview of the package itself; use 'Get a package version' for one release.
get_package.name: get_package

parameters.description: The npm package to look up, exactly as it is installed. Scoped names include the scope.
parameters.name: package

parameters.description: Turn on to return the start of the package's readme alongside the rest, up to 4,000 characters. Off by default, because a readme is long and most steps do not need it.
parameters.name: include_readme

get_package_dependencies.description: List what a release depends on as one flat list, each row carrying the version range and which group it came from. npm splits these across four fields keyed by package name, which a workflow cannot walk without knowing the names already, so this is the action that answers 'does this still depend on lodash?' in one step. Choose which groups to include.
get_package_dependencies.display_str_template: Get the dependencies of the npm package {0}.
get_package_dependencies.name: get_package_dependencies

parameters.description: The npm package to look up, exactly as it is installed. Scoped names include the scope.
parameters.name: package

parameters.description: Which release to read. Choose a version number, or a release channel such as 'latest' or 'next', which always resolves to whatever that channel points at today. Fill in the package first and this list loads. Defaults to 'latest'.
parameters.name: version

parameters.description: Which groups to include. Choose none to include all four.
parameters.name: dependency_types

options.label: Dependencies: needed to run the package
Dev dependencies: needed only to build or test it
Peer dependencies: expected in the host project
Optional dependencies: installed if they can be

Pick one of the standard periods, or set a start and end date for anything else. The answer names the days npm actually counted, so a partly covered period still reads honestly.

get_registry_downloads.description: Count how many packages the whole npm registry served over a period. It is the denominator for any 'what share of npm is this?' question, and the way to tell whether a package's quiet week was its own or everyone's.

This is the action that answers 'has anyone moved to version 5 yet?'. npm publishes this breakdown for the last 7 days only, so the period is fixed.

Versions are ordered by semantic version rather than as text, so 1.10.0 sits above 1.9.0 and a release sits above its own release candidates.

search_packages.description: Search npm and get back the matches with their weekly and monthly downloads, how many packages depend on them, and npm's own quality, popularity and maintenance scores. The search qualifiers are separate fields here, so filtering to one maintainer or one scope, or leaving out anything deprecated, needs no query syntax.

packages.description: Shopify GraphQL Client - A lightweight generic GraphQL JS client to interact with Shopify GraphQL APIs
packages.name: @shopify/graphql-client

search_packages.name: search_packages

parameters.description: What to search for. Can be left empty if you filter by author, maintainer, scope or keyword instead.
parameters.name: text

parameters.description: Only packages whose manifest names this npm user as the author.
parameters.name: author

parameters.description: Only packages this npm user can publish. Broader than author: it covers everything they help look after.
parameters.name: maintainer

parameters.description: Only packages published under this scope. The '@' is optional.
parameters.name: scope

parameters.description: Only packages tagged with these keywords, separated by commas. A package must carry all of them.
parameters.name: keywords

parameters.description: Kinds of package to keep out of the results. Choose none to search everything.
parameters.name: exclude

options.label: Packages with a known security advisory

parameters.description: Narrow the results to packages in these states, which is how you audit for them. Choose none for no such restriction.
parameters.name: require

options.label: Only unstable packages, meaning below version 1.0.0
Only packages with a known security advisory

parameters.description: How much npm's quality score counts towards the ranking, from 0 to 1. Quality covers tests, documentation and a stable release history. Leave empty for npm's own balance.
parameters.name: quality

parameters.description: How much downloads and dependents count towards the ranking, from 0 to 1. Raise it to favour the well-established package over the neat new one. Leave empty for npm's own balance.
parameters.name: popularity

parameters.description: How much recent activity counts towards the ranking, from 0 to 1. Raise it to favour packages that are still being worked on. Leave empty for npm's own balance.
parameters.name: maintenance

parameters.name: offset

description: Look up anything on the public npm registry. Read a package's details, licence and maintainers, walk its release history, open one version for its dependencies and tarball, check what each release channel points at, search npm with its own quality and popularity scores, and track download counts by day, by version or against other packages. No account or API key is required.
